stories.topic: 1869: The Year India Was Wired Into the World
stories.summary: The Suez Canal opened in 1869. Before it, ships from London went around the Cape of Good Hope, and having come that far they might as well continue to Calcutta. After it, the route ran through Gibraltar, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea straight to Bombay. In the same years the telegraph arrived, cutting a London-Bombay message to about four hours, and the railroad spread. Britain's Companies Act, Contract Act and Evidence Act reached Bombay within a couple of years of passing in London. The Bombay Stock Exchange opened in 1874. When the American Civil War cut US cotton supplies to Britain, a whole new cotton trade appeared: grown in Gujarat and Maharashtra, shipped through Bombay to London. This first modernisation, matching the first globalisation, lasted roughly from 1869 to 1913.
stories.insight: Modern India has an earlier birth date than 1947 or 1991: a burst of connectivity, technology and market institutions in the 1860s-70s. Ajay thinks Indian history undervalues this period because the nationalists oversold their case. He does not pine for colonial rule, but argues history should be read 'cold and clear.'
stories.quote: It's like the entire institutional package and the technological capability of the Industrial Revolution was seeded into India all at once.

stories.topic: Malaria, Gin and Tonic, and American Ice
stories.summary: Malaria was a huge problem in India, and the defence was quinine. Quinine was too bitter to take on its own, so it was put into tonic water, and gin and tonic became a popular drink in India. A gin and tonic needs ice, and there were no fridges in the 19th century. So factories making ice sprang up in the American Midwest.
stories.insight: A health problem in India created an industry on the other side of the world. No planner arranged it; trade and prices connected the two. Amit tells it as a parallel to the Civil War cotton boom.
stories.quote: No fridges. Where will the ice come from? America will make the ice. So the wonders of global capitalism.

stories.topic: India in 1947 Was Freer Than You Think
stories.summary: Ajay argues that the 1947-62 growth was decent partly because social tension eased. The world war, the freedom-movement strife and Partition were over, and the new Republic, its Constitution and leaders like Nehru and Patel gave the private sector confidence. In 1947 the state intervened only modestly in the economy, the civil service was the best India has ever had, and for a while the current and capital accounts were fully convertible. Then, day after day, restrictions crept in and a vast repressive machinery was built. Amit adds that the roughly five percent growth of this period looks good only against the war years, and terrible against what Korea and Southeast Asia achieved.
stories.insight: Good-looking growth numbers can hide deteriorating policy. Ajay's point is that the outcomes looked decent while the inputs were steadily getting worse.
stories.quote: We've never had a better civil service in India than was present in 1947.

stories.summary: Before 1914 nobody needed a passport anywhere in the world. Royals wrote letters to each other asking for special treatment for their friends, but ordinary people could simply travel and migrate. Capital controls did not exist until Adolf Hitler introduced them in Germany. In India, restrictions on trade and capital flows began as a British wartime measure in 1939. The Treaty of Versailles included a clause restoring passport-free travel, and international conferences tried to bring it back into the 1960s. Soviet Russia blocked every attempt because it did not want its citizens leaving and never returning. Only the European Union has partly restored that old freedom.
stories.insight: Many controls we treat as permanent features of the world are emergency measures that never ended. 'Temporary' wartime losses of freedom tend to become normal.
stories.quote: Did you know that before 1914 there were no passports anywhere in the world?

stories.summary: India in 1947 was a bold political experiment: universal suffrage in a country where women's literacy was six percent. Then came the 1962 China war, Nehru's death in 1964, the 1965 war with Pakistan, two droughts in a row, famine, and begging the US for PL 480 food aid. In 1969 the banks were nationalised. The 1971 war was a 'nationalist wet dream' but a huge economic burden. FERA followed in 1973. The glow of the Bangladesh war and Indira Gandhi's big election win soon gave way to double-digit inflation, the JP agitation and the Emergency. Ajay notes Indira was the first Indian prime minister whom political scientists classify as a populist.
stories.insight: There was a real chance India would become 'another disgusting authoritarian third world country' or fall into civil war, and the skeptics of Indian democracy nearly looked right. It is a reminder of how fragile the Indian project was.
stories.quote: In a country in 1947 where women's literacy was six percent, there was the audacity of thinking that we'll have universal suffrage.

stories.topic: Book a Scooter for Your Daughter's Wedding
stories.summary: Amit reads from Shruti Rajagopalan's essay on the Indira years. The 14 largest banks were nationalised overnight by ordinance, along with coal, copper, general insurance and unprofitable textile firms. There were land ceilings and import tariffs above 350%, and the top income tax rate was 97.75%. The underground economy may have grown larger than the formal one. By the late 1970s it was almost impossible to start a business or close a failing one. The joke of the time was to book a scooter for a daughter early, so it would arrive by her wedding. Amit argues Indira did not even believe in this socialism and used it to tilt left against the Congress syndicate.
stories.insight: Amit's provocative claim is that Indira's economic regulations did more damage than the Emergency. They kept millions in poverty for decades longer than necessary and blocked the labour-intensive manufacturing boom that could have come before China's.
stories.quote: India was the one country in the world where a secondhand car cost more than a new car. Because a new car would take years to get delivered.

stories.topic: Nehru's Daughter Was Embarrassed to Be a Tyrant
stories.summary: Ajay says leaked diplomatic material from the Emergency shows Indira Gandhi was embarrassed about it, and elections were only a matter of time. The 1977 elections were genuinely free and fair, with no intimidation of the opposition and no booth tampering. Amit adds that she expected to win and that Sanjay Gandhi did not want her to call the elections. Ajay replies that it went deeper: Nehru's daughter could not bear becoming one more third-world tyrant.
stories.insight: India 'lucked out.' What saved its democracy at the brink was partly one leader's sense of embarrassment, a reminder of how much rested on personal character rather than institutions.
stories.quote: It was only Sanjay Gandhi's mother who could have declared the emergency, and it was only Jawaharlal Nehru's daughter who could have declared elections.

stories.topic: Three Gujaratis Turn the Ship in 1977
stories.summary: When the Janata Party came to power, three Gujaratis became the country's most powerful people: Morarji Desai as Prime Minister, H.M. Patel as Finance Minister and D.T. Lakdawala as Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission. They were not radical reformers, but they had a feel for how markets work. Lakdawala had always been at Bombay University, away from Delhi's leftist economics establishment. Patel had grown up near Amul and the cooperative movement. Through small measures and key staffing choices they began liberalising. Careful econometrics dates India's growth acceleration to 1979. Indira, on her return, carried these ideas further, and Rajiv Gandhi pushed them more.
stories.insight: 1991 did not come out of nowhere. Growth picked up more than a decade earlier, once the private sector began cautiously trusting the state again.
stories.quote: The best ideas always incubated far away. The further away you are from power, the more clearly you see.

stories.topic: The Reformers Who Came Home With No Promise
stories.summary: Ajay compares two dark periods, 1927-47 and 1962-77. In the first, the British Empire looked invincible, yet the best Indians wrote longhand letters and debated rival ideas of India, so that people and documents were ready in 1947. In the second, many gave up and emigrated. Ajay was born in 1966 and has heard these stories from his elders. Manmohan Singh came back after his PhD with no idea he would become finance minister or prime minister. Amit adds that Singh asked his young mentee Montek Singh Ahluwalia to come back and work for the country, and Montek left the World Bank. Vijay Kelkar 'felt obliged to say, Yes, sir, I will,' and packed his bags. Amit also notes that just as we remember those who fought, we should remember those who didn't. Ajay says most people were simply appeasers.
stories.insight: Big reforms rest on years of unrewarded preparation by people who chose to stay and build knowledge and community without knowing whether it would ever pay off.
stories.quote: He had no idea. Nobody would have bet on a million to one odds that this was going to happen.

stories.topic: Two Speeches a Week at the Finance Ministry
stories.summary: When Ajay worked in the Ministry of Finance, every joint secretary in the Department of Economic Affairs gave two conference speeches every week. The aim was to show the private sector capable people, a way of thinking, a vision and a strategy that it would respect.
stories.insight: Reform is partly a matter of signalling. The private sector invests when it can see a competent crew with a plan running the state.
stories.quote: Every joint secretary would go out and do two conference speeches every week. Because part of the story was showing a capability, was showing a thought process.

stories.summary: In 2008-09, with Manmohan Singh as PM and P. Chidambaram as Finance Minister, India was handling the global financial crisis well. Then came the Mumbai terror attacks. Home Minister Shivraj Patil could not cope, so Singh moved Chidambaram to Home, leaving Finance empty. Singh would have held it himself, but he needed an operation that January. Sonia Gandhi then installed Pranab Mukherjee, a socialist of the Indira-era 1970s, who brought in policies like retrospective taxation. Around 2013 he was 'kicked upstairs' to the presidency and Chidambaram returned. The Jaitley ministry after 2014 initially showed continuity, but from 2015 politics took over. Ajay rejects the bad-luck explanation. He argues the post-1991 reformers never rebuilt the oppressive laws and machinery of government, so everything depended on a few individuals.
stories.insight: A chain of accidents can derail an economy only if the system depends on who happens to sit in which chair. Ajay's lesson is to put freedom into laws and organisation design, not to rely on good people.
stories.quote: Manmohan Singh wanted his best man on the job, that was Chidambaram. That meant the finance ministry was now empty.

recommendations.creator: Tripurdaman Singh
recommendations.context: Amit's formal recommendation at the end of the episode; the author has been on The Seen and the Unseen twice.
recommendations.reason: It shows how India's First Amendment, unlike America's, was a blow against free speech. The Lok Sabha debates reveal Nehru taking illiberal positions to silence his communist rivals, a great statesman undone by hubris.

recommendations.item: Nehru: The Debates that Defined India
recommendations.creator: Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
recommendations.context: Amit's second end-of-episode recommendation.
recommendations.reason: Nehru's exchanges with Jinnah, Syama Prasad Mookerjee and Patel show fine minds disagreeing in good faith. Amit finds this spirit of 'assume goodwill', lost in today's public discourse, deeply inspiring.

recommendations.item: The quest for economic freedom in India
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Amit reads passages from it about the Indira Gandhi years.
recommendations.reason: He calls it 'absolutely magisterial'. It catalogues the nationalisations, 350% tariffs, 97.75% income tax and the scarcity-era jokes of that period.

recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan / Mercatus Center
recommendations.context: Mentioned while discussing the people who prepared the 1991 reforms over many years.
recommendations.reason: Its chronicles and oral histories of the reformers 'fill me with awe'. They show that the reformers had worked for a decade and a half before 1991.

recommendations.item: The Economic Legacies of Colonial Rule in India
recommendations.creator: Tirthankar Roy
recommendations.context: Vinay Sitapati sent it to Amit; he reads its conclusion aloud after Ajay's account of 1860s Bombay.
recommendations.reason: A 'fabulous essay' arguing the colonial economy was open to trade, capital and migration. It says economic nationalists misread payments to the British as a 'drain' when they were the price of tapping global markets for skills and capital.

recommendations.item: Planners vs. Searchers in Foreign Aid
recommendations.creator: William Easterly
recommendations.context: Easterly's paper for the ADB, quoted at length to explain what went wrong after 1947.
recommendations.reason: It frames the key contrast: planners impose top-down answers, while searchers find solutions by trial, error and feedback. Amit says poverty has only ever been ended by searchers.

recommendations.creator: Richard Eaton
recommendations.context: Cited via Vinay Sitapati's argument about pre-colonial India.
recommendations.reason: A 'magnificent book' adored by the Mughal historians on Amit's show. It suggests global trade shifted power to the port cities and weakened the centralised empire.

recommendations.item: Half-Lion: How PV Narasimha Rao Transformed India
recommendations.creator: Vinay Sitapati
recommendations.context: Amit calls Sitapati's books great while introducing his idea that 1991 was a 're-liberalisation'.
recommendations.reason: Background on Narasimha Rao, who staked his political capital on the 1991 reforms.

recommendations.creator: Vinay Sitapati
recommendations.context: Named alongside Half-Lion as Sitapati's other great book.
recommendations.reason: Same enthusiasm for Sitapati's work as an interpreter of post-Independence political history.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a 'great book'; Ajay explains why he and Kelkar wrote it (first edition 2019, second 2022).
recommendations.reason: It sets out the first principles of state capacity, public administration, law, freedom, market failure and regulation. Ajay says the 1991-2011 reformers lacked this knowledge, which left their reforms fragile.

recommendations.creator: Manmohan Singh
recommendations.context: Ajay on how Indian economic thinking began to change.
recommendations.reason: One of the first works to challenge India's 'export pessimism'. It argued that exporting depends on incentives, prices and exchange rates, not on anything peculiar to India.

recommendations.creator: Arun Shourie
recommendations.context: Ajay on the thinkers who exposed the failures of Indian socialism.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says Shourie 'does not get enough recognition'. He worked out many ideas credited to Western scholars first, and laid bare the venality of the socialist state.

recommendations.creator: Angus Maddison
recommendations.context: Shown on screen while explaining why the world is not zero-sum.
recommendations.reason: They show world GDP shooting up around 1800 and economic freedom tracking prosperity country by country, including India after 1991 and China after Deng.

recommendations.creator: John Stossel
recommendations.context: Used to explain voluntary exchange.
recommendations.reason: A simple illustration that both sides gain in a voluntary trade: you thank the barista and the barista thanks you.

recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Invoked when discussing the collapse of the Soviet Union.
recommendations.reason: Captures the post-Cold War sense that liberal democracy might be history's endpoint. Amit warns that the 70% of Indians born after the Berlin Wall fell have forgotten those lessons.

recommendations.creator: Johan Norberg
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes to support Amit's rebuttal of the 'look at Scandinavia' argument.
recommendations.reason: Backs his claim that the Nordic countries became rich under free markets first and built their welfare states afterwards.

recommendations.creator: Speranta Dumitru
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Ajay's account of the world before passports.
recommendations.reason: Covers the history behind his point that passports and controls on movement began as wartime measures and were never rolled back.

recommendations.item: Pandit's Mind (1951 Time magazine cover story on Nehru)
recommendations.creator: Time magazine
recommendations.context: Amit quotes it to trace Nehru's intellectual influences.
recommendations.reason: A vivid portrait of how Fabian socialism and Brahminical contempt for the 'Banya' shaped Nehru's distrust of capitalism.

recommendations.creator: Madhav Khosla
recommendations.context: Cited for the idea that the Constitution was a pedagogic exercise.
recommendations.reason: Helps explain the elite, top-down mindset of the founders, who felt they had to teach the nation how to think.

recommendations.creator: Puja Mehra
recommendations.context: Amit borrows Mehra's phrase for India's post-2011 slowdown.
recommendations.reason: The book-length account of how growth stalled, a process Amit dates from 2008.

recommendations.creator: Lawrence H White
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes; not discussed in the conversation.
recommendations.reason: Background on the economic ideas, such as Fabian socialism and central planning, whose influence on India the episode traces.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit sends listeners there instead of repeating the details.
recommendations.reason: Covers in depth what 1991 achieved and what it left undone, including factor markets and agriculture.

recommendations.item: India's Greatest Civil Servant (Episode 167, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Narayani Basu
recommendations.context: Mentioned when describing how Patel and VP Menon unified India.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'a great episode' on what he describes as a 'fast track colonisation' of India in a couple of years.

recommendations.item: The Forgotten Greatness of PV Narasimha Rao (Episode 283, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
recommendations.context: Mentioned while discussing the long preparation behind 1991.
recommendations.reason: A deeper look at Rao and the reformers around him.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Episode 285, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
recommendations.context: Amit cites Montek as underscoring that 1991 was years in the making.
recommendations.reason: An insider's account of the 'silent revolution' that built up from the late 1970s.

recommendations.item: India's Lost Decade (Episode 116, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Puja Mehra
recommendations.context: Mentioned while summarising India's post-2008 slowdown.
recommendations.reason: A longer conversation on what went wrong after 2008.

recommendations.item: The Art and Science of Economic Policy (Episode 154, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The recording session behind Amit's anecdote about Vijay Kelkar.
recommendations.reason: Kelkar and Ajay discussing their book on economic policy.

recommendations.item: The First Assault on Our Constitution (Episode 194) and Nehru's Debates (Episode 262), The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh (and Adeel Hussain)
recommendations.context: Companions to his two book recommendations; he calls the second one of his 'sleeper hits.'
recommendations.reason: Long-form conversations with the authors of Sixteen Stormy Days and Nehru: The Debates that Defined India.

recommendations.item: Newton the Alchemist. Gandhi the Black Swan (Episode 7, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced before Amit examines Nehru's intellectual influences.
recommendations.reason: That episode traced Gandhi's intellectual influences; this one does the same for Nehru.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit reframes freedom as consent. Two questions usually kept apart, 'how should I live?' and 'how should the state relate to society?', get the same answer: consent is everything and coercion is the ultimate evil. You can arrive at this from first principles (individual autonomy, John Locke's self-ownership) or from consequences (freedom produces the best outcomes). He also flags the 'grand liberal paradox': to protect our rights we need a state, and the state itself takes some of those rights through taxes and its monopoly on violence.
core_ideas.quote: The answer is consent. That consent is everything and coercion is the ultimate evil.

core_ideas.explanation: Our brains evolved in scarce, tribal times, so we assume one person's gain is another's loss. But in every voluntary exchange both sides gain, so more exchange means more total wealth. Angus Maddison's charts show world GDP exploding around 1800 with industrialisation and trade. Nitin Pai's estimate is that after 1991, each 1% of GDP growth lifted about three million Indians out of poverty, so 300-400 million in all. That makes freedom a humanitarian issue, not just an economic one.
core_ideas.quote: Every voluntary transaction leaves both people better off. And therefore the more voluntary transactions there are, the more the wealth of the world goes up.

core_ideas.explanation: We tend to assume anything complex and beautiful must have a designer. Amit suggests religion itself may be an example of this delusion. Yet languages, economies, societies and natural selection all emerge without a central planner. In Adam Ferguson's words, they are 'the products of human action and not human design.'
core_ideas.quote: Economists have this beautiful term spontaneous order. Languages, economies, societies, natural selection itself does not need a central planner or a designer.

core_ideas.explanation: William Easterly's distinction. A planner thinks he already knows the answers and treats poverty as an engineering problem. A searcher admits ignorance, sees poverty as a tangle of political, social, historical and institutional factors, and finds solutions by trial, error and feedback. Firms in markets and politicians accountable to voters are searchers. Ajay sums it up as 'discovery, not design.'
core_ideas.quote: Historically poverty has never been ended by central planners. It is only ended by searchers.

core_ideas.explanation: People can survive under unfreedom, even in a concentration camp. But once individual agency is taken away, a society stops thinking and creating, and art, science and business fall into dull despondency. A poor country needs the opposite: a bubbling of optimism, invention and new businesses, and that only comes from freedom.
core_ideas.quote: What we need is an effervescence of optimism, of creativity, of invention, of people starting a business, of people coming up with a new business model.

core_ideas.concept: India's 'Golden Age' GDP Was an Illusion
core_ideas.explanation: Pre-industrial India had a large share of world GDP only because it had good weather, agriculture and a huge population. Output per person was abysmal everywhere then. Ajay warns against nostalgia: old India had extreme poverty and cruelty, little political development and no rule of law.
core_ideas.quote: It was not a golden age. There were levels of poverty and deprivation and cruelty that were in India that were out of the world. There was very little political development, there was no rule of law.

core_ideas.explanation: This is Vinay Sitapati's argument, relayed by Amit. Before 1947 the port cities were already plugged into global trade, and Richard Eaton suggests such trade shaped power in India even earlier. So the real break with the past was Nehru's Fabian socialism and central planning, and 1991 was a return to openness rather than its invention.
core_ideas.quote: We should think of the liberalization of ninety one as a re-liberalization of ninety one. His point is that it was Nehru's Fabian Socialism and Central Planning that was a break from the past.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit sees a constant tug of war between state and society. In 1947 three forces pushed towards the centre. Politically, the country seemed to be falling apart, so leaders wanted the centre to hold. Socially, Ambedkar saw villages as dens of localism and caste and wanted a transformative constitution; Madhav Khosla calls it a pedagogic exercise. Economically, Nehru distrusted profit and capitalists. Amit sympathises with all three, but thinks elites erred in believing a liberal society could be imposed from above.
core_ideas.quote: Those who wanted liberal values and a free society, to say that that can only be imposed from the top down, whereas I continue to believe, though it would have been difficult to see then or argue then, that it can only happen from the bottom up.

core_ideas.explanation: The tragedy of Indian socialism was not being wrong but refusing to correct course. Some of the smartest people available met each failure with more controls. Ajay blames the Indian intellectual class as a whole, seduced by state power and the Soviet model, for creating the climate in which Nehru's and Indira's excesses could happen.
core_ideas.quote: It is okay to be wrong. It is not okay to be impervious to the evidence.

core_ideas.explanation: Indian elites once believed India could never export. Manmohan Singh's thesis argued that exports depend on prices, incentives and exchange rates. Change came slowly. In 1947 India, with Gandhi, Tagore, Ramanujan and Nehru, had more intellectual capital than any other poor country, so East Asia racing ahead was deeply embarrassing. That shock pushed the best of the elite, like Vijay Kelkar who started out leftist, back to first principles.
core_ideas.quote: At the time people believed that because our skins are brown we'll never be able to export. And Manmohan Singh was one of the early people to say no. It's about incentives, it's about prices, it's about exchange rates.

core_ideas.explanation: Growth comes from the private sector committing its time, its children's careers and its money to building firms. That happens when business feels optimistic and safe about where India is heading. Growth follows changes in this mood, which is why small reforms in 1977 showed up as faster growth by 1979.
core_ideas.quote: Always and always and always there is only one source of economic growth and that is the private sector.

core_ideas.explanation: Every country has four elites: political and bureaucratic, business, intellectual, and cultural. They need a working bargain. From 1991 to 2011 the bargain was this: the state was full of 'landmines', but when business hit one, someone competent listened and often fixed it. That fell apart as the state's deeds fell short of its words. Ajay's summary statistic: there was less freedom in 2010 than in 2000, and less in 2020 than in 2010.
core_ideas.quote: Every now and then things will go wrong, but I will have the ability to file a bug report and I will have the ability to find some recourse.

core_ideas.explanation: The post-1991 reforms left the oppressive machinery of government intact. Ajay says the laws of 2008-09 were more oppressive than those of 1991. Good people ran an old apparatus better, but never rebuilt it, so one reshuffle could derail everything. His counterexample is the US under Donald Trump, where much of government carried on as usual because its institutions have quality of their own. Real reform means writing freedom into laws and designing better organisations.
core_ideas.quote: What was keeping the ship aloft were certain individuals, which to me is an unacceptable and fragile way of building a country.

core_ideas.concept: Dig In Without Promise of Reward
core_ideas.explanation: In both 1927-47 and 1962-77, India's prospects looked hopeless. The best people stayed, built knowledge and built community, without any guarantee of power or success. When the openings came in 1947 and 1991, they were ready. Amit links this to Lincoln's line about spending most of your time sharpening the axe.
core_ideas.quote: People should not ask for fate to step out of the page of history and shake your hand. People should just be quiet and dig in and work hard and you have no right to ask for any reward.

core_ideas.concept: Freedom Is Not Inevitable, and Neither Is Despair
core_ideas.explanation: Promising beginnings can turn ugly: Deng's 1978 opening led to today's China, the fall of the USSR led to today's Russia, and Weimar's freedom led to Nazi Germany. But the reverse also happens. Germany and Japan, once called inherently obedient or militaristic, became 'beautiful countries.' Be cautious, never complacent, and keep thinking and talking.
core_ideas.quote: The world is a rich and wonderful place and progress can always happen.

core_ideas.concept: Why Scandinavia Doesn't Refute Free Markets
core_ideas.explanation: People point to Nordic welfare states as proof that freedom isn't needed. Amit's answer has two parts. First, these countries remain very free for starting and running businesses and for personal and social life. Second, they became rich while they were essentially free markets, and could afford welfare only after reaching a high standard of living.
core_ideas.quote: All of them became rich when they were basically free markets. And once they had brought their standard of living to a certain level, then they could do their welfare statism.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit opens by explaining that a young cat is mewing in the background, because 'it sounds like the wailing of all the dispossessed and the hungry and the starving through these many, many years of India's tormented journey.'

Around 2008 Amit pitched a book called 'Freedom After Midnight', a play on Lapierre and Collins's Freedom at Midnight, arguing that 1947 brought only political freedom. He never wrote it 'because I'm a lazy bum', and the New India Foundation rejected the proposal anyway.

Ajay lists the dangers of the 1940s, including 'one minor character, Subhash Chandra Bose, threatening armed conflict in India.' Amit objects, and Ajay retracts: 'Fine. So scratch the Subhash Chandra Bose.'
Ajay praises the EU for restoring passport-free movement 'between France, Germany, and Belgium and UK. Oh, scratch that, not UK.'
On planners who answered every failure with more controls, Ajay says they insisted 'the floggings will continue until the morale improves.'

After a toilet break while recording with Amit, Vijay Kelkar pointed a finger and said he had one piece of advice. Amit braced for great wisdom: 'Every time you pass a toilet, enter it.' Amit: 'So that is, you know, the wise passing on their wisdom to younger folks.'

Amit, on the Janata reformers coming from outside Delhi: 'Maybe India's next intellectual revolution can happen far from Delhi in lonely Karjat.' Ajay: 'The further away you are from power, the more clearly you see.'

Ajay is pleased that viewers are often left wondering, 'Do you guys agree on this or do you guys disagree on this?' Amit closes by telling him that since he brought no recommendations, he owes double next week.
Nehru to J.R.D. Tata: 'Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.'

Time magazine, 1951, on Nehru: 'Beatrice and Sidney Webb, the godparents of Fabian socialism, are in a truer sense his creators than Vishnu and Shiva.' The piece also describes his contempt for the 'Banya civilization' of the capitalist West.

Harold Laski's influence on Nehru: John Kenneth Galbraith said Laski was at the centre of Nehru's thinking, and Ramachandra Guha quoted an unnamed wit saying that at every cabinet meeting 'there was an empty seat and Harold Laski sat on it.'
C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji), whom Nehru ignored, understood the power of freedom and looked not to Russia but to the success of America.

P. Chidambaram's verdict, quoted by Amit: 'India suspected capitalists, it suspected the profit motive, and it tried to nail it down, block it, and thought that all growth would come from government planning.' By the late 1980s, Korea was a miracle economy and India 'a stagnant slow trot.'
Abraham Lincoln's line, as Amit quotes it: 'If I have six hours to cut a tree, I'll spend the first five sharpening the axe.' Amit applies it to the reformers who prepared for years before 1991.
Adam Ferguson's description of spontaneous order: 'the products of human action and not human design.'
